audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both quoted passages are verbatim in copies we hold at the stated locators (Google Books PA21 snippet JSONs; Saltzman 2022 txt at the p.59/60 break). (2) The deciding source is the right one: Yang, Yang & O'Grady 2020 is the standard and only full reference grammar of Jejueo (Glottolog rank 'grammar', xii+302 pp), and the statement sits in its phonology chapter (ch.2, pp.15-36). The weakness is custody, not choice: we hold a snippet, not the page. (3) The instrumental study the grammar cites for its prosody claim, Lee Sook-hyang 2014 (Phonetics and Speech Sciences 6(4)), was downloaded open-access and read: it defines the Jejueo accentual phrase's basic pattern as <L+H L+Ha> 'like Seoul dialect' within the K-ToBI intonational hierarchy, i.e. phrase-level tonal prominence with no word stress or lexical pitch accent, which directly confirms the 'phrasal' coding and the the primary-stress rule. sources.quote: Abstract (p.117): 'The results showed that like Seoul dialect <L +H L+ Ha> pattern could be the basic pattern of accentual phase in Jeju dialect even though several differences were observed in the realization of each tone ... unlike Seoul dialect, most speakers showed <H L+ Ha> pattern in an accentual phrase beginning with a strong consonant.' Conclusion (p.122): '두 개의 실험을 통해 제주어 강세구의 억양기본패턴을 서울말과 같이 <L+H L+Ha>로 정의하였다' [Through two experiments the basic intonation pattern of the Jejueo accentual phrase was defined as <L+H L+Ha>, as in Seoul Korean]. sources.note: One second-hand sentence: Cheju, like Seoul and Chonnam, has no lexical F0 (pitch accent) contrast; consistent with the catalog's jeju1234 coding (phrasal). The F0 effect reported for Cheju is the laryngeal-category (lax vs tense/aspirated) cue, not lexical tone. Chonnam and Hamgyong are also named in passing (Chonnam: AP-level phonologization like Seoul; Hamgyong: preserves lexical pitch), both second-hand, no catalog codes supplied.
